> **▶ [Solve it on TrueInterview](https://trueinterview.io/questions/data-labeling-task-scheduler)** — free, no card: a runnable editor, the sample and hidden tests, a judged verdict, and the reference solution.

## Problem

A data-labeling platform coordinates three kinds of entities: labeling tasks, AI models, and human annotators. Every entity is identified by a string ID whose numbering starts at 1.

Implement `build_balanced_schedule(totalTask, totalModel, totalHuman, k)`, where the four integers define the available IDs and the workload requirement:

* The tasks are `"t1"`, `"t2"`, ..., `"t{totalTask}"`.
* The models are `"m1"`, `"m2"`, ..., `"m{totalModel}"`.
* The human annotators are `"h1"`, `"h2"`, ..., `"h{totalHuman}"`.

A single assignment is written as `[task, model, human]` and means that this human labels this task with the help of this model. One task is allowed to show up in several assignments, so it may be labeled by more than one human and combined with more than one model.

Produce **any valid schedule** — a list of assignments — that meets all of these conditions:

* Every human is part of at least `k` assignments.
* No human is assigned to the same task twice.
* Each assignment only refers to task, model, and human IDs inside the ranges defined above.

When no schedule can satisfy these conditions, return an empty list.

Example 1:

```text
Input: totalTask = 3, totalModel = 1, totalHuman = 2, k = 2

Output: [["t1", "m1", "h1"], ["t2", "m1", "h2"], ["t2", "m1", "h1"], ["t3", "m1", "h2"]]
```

Explanation: This is just one acceptable answer. Each annotator handles 2 different tasks — `"h1"` takes `"t1"` and `"t2"`, and `"h2"` takes `"t2"` and `"t3"` — so nobody repeats a task and both meet the minimum of `k = 2` assignments.

Example 2:

```text
Input: totalTask = 1, totalModel = 1, totalHuman = 1, k = 1

Output: [["t1", "m1", "h1"]]
```

Example 3:

```text
Input: totalTask = 2, totalModel = 3, totalHuman = 3, k = 2

Output: [["t1", "m1", "h1"], ["t2", "m1", "h2"], ["t1", "m1", "h3"], ["t2", "m1", "h1"], ["t1", "m1", "h2"], ["t2", "m1", "h3"]]
```

Constraints:

* $$1 \le totalTask,\ totalModel,\ totalHuman \le 100$$
* $$0 \le k \le totalTask$$

## Follow-ups

Extensions an interviewer may raise after the main task:

- Extend the schedule so that (model, human) pairs are also spread evenly, with every pairwise combination balanced, on top of the existing constraints.
- Extend the solution to a streaming variant in which new tasks arrive each day; update the schedule incrementally without restarting, and make sure each human handles at most one task per day.

## Hints

<details>
<summary>Hint 1</summary>

Think of this as constructing assignments so that the load is spread evenly, with each task, model, and human appearing in a controlled number of triples.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Hint 2</summary>

Use a systematic round-robin or modular pattern to generate triples so counts stay balanced, rather than searching randomly.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Hint 3</summary>

Check the feasibility conditions on totalTask, totalModel, totalHuman, and k first, and watch duplicate triples and cases where balance is impossible.

</details>
